_doc: RULINGS on the crosswalk's proposals. tools/read_land_sales.py --build folds this file onto resident_crosswalk.json; --check refuses a ruling that names a spelling the register does not hold, or a person the proposal did not name. This file is HAND-AUTHORED and is the one file under data/research/land_sales/ that is not derived from the deposit — a judgement is not a derivation, and the project does not pretend otherwise.
why_this_exists: build_resident_crosswalk() applies ONE mechanical rule: the surname agrees, the residents layer holds exactly one person of that surname, and the first forename agrees in full or as an initial. That rule proposes; it does not decide. tools/spend_land_sales.py's own rule 1 says so in as many words — 'ONLY WHAT THE CROSSWALK ALREADY DECLARED. This pass re-adjudicates nothing.' — so between the proposal and the card there was nobody. T-0700 is the ticket that noticed it, against the nine spellings the ring townships added (T-0676).
the_ruling_rule: A proposal is UPHELD only where the town's own record of the person carries something the register's row can be checked against BEYOND a bare name — a middle initial the register repeats, a trade the purchase is consistent with, a second document, or the register's own Residence column. Where the town holds nothing but a name read once off a post-office letter list, the proposal rests on the residents layer being THIN rather than on the two records agreeing: an uncalled-for letter says a correspondent thought the name reachable at Chicago, and a tract entry says a name entered ground, and two name-only readings do not make an identity. Such a proposal is REFUSED. A ruling never raises a grade, never mints a resident, and never asserts a residence; a refusal retracts what a pass had already written. T-0993 adds the ruling that goes the other way. `upheld` and `refused` can only adjudicate a proposal; a reading the forename rule structurally cannot reach — a man's middle name printed where his forename belongs — had no way to be ruled on at all, and the gate called a ruling on it 'a ruling on nothing'. `named` gives the match instead of taking it away, and it is held to the mirror of the same guards: only where the surname gathered rivals and the forename failed to choose among them, only onto one of those rivals, and never onto a surname-only purchaser, which this domain refuses however well the tract agrees.
scope: The nine purchaser spellings the ring deposit (T-0676) added, ruled under T-0700; the twenty-six the first deposit matched, ruled under T-0850 — sixteen upheld, ten refused; and, under T-0990, COHORT A — the fourteen proposals whose crosswalk match is `initial_agrees` AND whose `rivals[]` is non-empty, which is where the mechanical rule is weakest: the layer holds a namesake of the surname and a forename INITIAL alone chose between them. Eleven upheld, three refused. What is left unruled is the rest of what T-0697 ADDED when the mechanical rule stopped requiring exactly one person of the surname; the count is on the crosswalk's own `ruled` block rather than in this sentence, and the next cohort is its own ticket. And, under T-0993, the ONE spelling the mechanical rule could never propose: BLANCHARD GURTREY, the six school-section rows ls0076-ls0081, NAMED onto blanchard_f_gantry — the register printing Francis Gurtrey Blanchard's middle name in the forename's place. That is a third ruling kind, `named`, and read_land_sales.py's gate guards it. A ruling the derivation later absorbs is moved to `retired[]` with the date, the ticket and the reason: retired, not deleted, because the argument is what the rule was written from. COHORT B, under T-0990 — the twenty-four proposals whose `rivals[]` is EMPTY, where the layer holds the surname exactly once and the mechanical rule had no namesake to choose among: twelve upheld, twelve refused. COHORT C1, under T-0990 — the seventeen surviving `forename_agrees` proposals whose purchaser spelling begins A, B or C, the first surname block of the sixty-six cohort B left: nine upheld, eight refused. Here the forename agrees IN FULL, so the forename itself decides nothing; what decides is whether the town holds the man in more than one INDEPENDENT kind of document, and whether one of those documents carries a token the register's row also carries — a middle initial, a trade the purchase is what you would predict from, or a date and place that bracket the entry.
ruled_by: the steward loop, under T-0700, T-0850, T-0990 and T-0993

ruled.reasoning: The initial alone would not carry it. What carries it is that the SAME register spells him PEARSONS HIRAM on twenty-eight other rows, one of which states COOK, and that the seventeen H rows are one hand at work: sixteen of them fall on a single day, 26 June 1835, in one township, T39N R13E, and eight of those in one section. A speculator buying half of section 10 and all four eighths of section 14 in an afternoon is the man the town already holds buying at the ring, not a second Pearsons who happens to share the county, the month and the surname.

The middle initial is the check the bare-name rule lacks, and it agrees: the town's man is Walter LOOMIS Newberry, attested at the American of 1835 and in both Fergus directories, and the register writes WALTER L. Six ring tracts entered on 26 and 27 June 1835 sit beside the town lots he was trading in the same season. Nothing here says he lived on any of it.

The town's James Whitlock is documented in four numbers of the Democrat between March and July 1835 AT A TRADE, and the trade is register of the land office. A land-office register entering a federal tract in June 1835 is the purchase the record would predict; the two readings are consistent in occupation as well as in name, which is the corroboration the mechanical rule could not see. The trade is what upholds this, and it is not evidence that he lived on the eighty acres in T38N R14E.

The middle initial agrees — the register writes CAMPBELL JAMES B and the town holds James B Campbell — and the town holds him across nine sources, from the poll lists of 1833-1835 to the old-settler notices, which is the densest record of the nine. Two tracts on one day, 8 August 1835, in T38N R14E and T38N R15E.

The town's record is a single post-office letter list — the weakest it accepts — and by the ruling rule that alone would refuse. It does not, because the list did not print a bare name: the Democrat of 28 January 1834 prints 'David P.Frame' and the register writes FRAME DAVID P. All three tokens agree, and a middle initial is exactly the second discriminator T-0696 says the crosswalks want. Upheld on the initial, and on nothing else: the entry proposes no residence, and the identity remains inferred.

The register itself supplies the check. Of the two rows entering the south-east quarter of section 12, T40N R13E on 10 April 1835, ls0912 states the purchaser's Residence as COOK — so the source that names him also places him in Cook County that spring, and the town's 1835 poll list places a Frank Dill at Chicago in the same year. Two records, an uncommon forename, and the county agreeing between them. WHAT THE RULING ALSO FOUND: the crosswalk was grading this proposal `inferred` and printing `residence_column: UNKNOWN`, because build_resident_crosswalk read the residence off the FIRST row of a spelling and the first row is the UNKNOWN one. The README's own rule is that a COOK row grades `documented` for residence in Cook County on the date of sale. The generator now reads every row of a spelling, and this proposal grades documented for that and nothing more — Cook County in 1835 reaches far beyond the town, and no residence in Chicago is asserted here.

SPENCER WILLIAM G is refused against William Spencer: the town's whole record of that man is one line of a post-office letter list — 'Spencer, William' in the Democrat's return of uncalled-for letters of 1 July 1835 — with no trade, no street and no second document, and the register adds a middle initial G the town has never seen. The mechanical rule fired because the residents layer holds exactly one Spencer, which is a fact about how thin the layer is and not about the man. Two name-only readings, disagreeing on the one token that could discriminate them.

WILSON JOHN L is refused against John Wilson. The town's John Wilson is known from a single return of uncalled-for letters, the Democrat of 28 January 1834, and nothing else names him; the register adds a middle initial L the town has never seen; and John Wilson is the commonest name in this corpus, so the rule's premise — exactly one of the surname in the residents layer — measures the layer and not the population. The three entries are also of 26 January and 10 March 1836, half a year past the town's last sight of the name. Refused on the ruling rule, and it would be refused on the initial alone.

The spelling T-0700 ruled on was the initial one; this is the full one, and it carries what that ruling leaned on. Twenty-eight rows over three years and 1,157 acres, one of them stating COOK, and the town's card names the trade outright: Hiram Pearsons is a speculator on Andreas's own list and on the poll of 1834. A register recording a man of that name buying half the ground he could reach is the trade the card already asserts, doing what the card says it did. Upholding the full spelling and refusing the initial one would also be incoherent, since T-0700 upheld PEARSONS H precisely BECAUSE these twenty-eight rows exist.

One quarter-section, 18 June 1836, and the only Elston in 431 purchaser spellings; the residents layer holds one too. What carries it is not the rarity but the bracket: the man is an advertiser in the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 and is still in the town for Fergus' directory of 1839, so the town's own record holds him on BOTH sides of the entry date rather than at one point near it. Nothing here says he lived on the tract or moved to it.

Two canal rows of 29 September 1830, one of them stating ILLINOIS. The date is the check. The town's own record bounds this man at Chicago by 31 December 1830 off the old-settler death notices, so the entry falls INSIDE the life the town holds rather than years to either side of it, and the ground he enters — the E2NE of section 9, which 18 standing roofs sit on — is the ground beside James Kinzie's E2NW of the same section entered the day before in the same sale. One agent's transaction on one day, and the town holds one Wolcott. What is NOT ruled is residence: a canal entry says a name took ground, and the ILLINOIS in the residence column is a state.

Thirteen parcels over the three days of the school-section auction, 22-24 October 1833, and the town's own tax list of 1833 names an Arthur Bronson in the same year. A town assessing a man and an auction of the town's own school section are the same twelve months and the same ground. The forename is also doing real work in this register rather than riding on a rare surname: BRONSON FREDERIC and BRONSON FREDERICK stand beside him on other rows, and the layer holds only the Arthur. The old-settler death notices are the second document.

The town's own poll list of 10 August 1833 and its tax list of 1833 both print Carver, David — two months before the school-section auction he buys at on 25 October 1833. Andreas gives him the trade, lumber merchant, and the register holds no other Carver. A townsman on the town's own rolls buying at the town's own sale, in the same season, is a correspondence with a date behind it and not merely a name.

The middle initial, printed on both sides. The register spells him CASEY EDWARD W; the town's tax list of 1833 and poll of 1834 both print 'Casey, Edward W.' This is the NEWBERRY WALTER L and CAMPBELL JAMES B carrier of T-0700 — a token the two records share that a namesake would have to share as well. He was corporation counsel and then clerk and collector across the municipal year, so the man was in the town at the October 1833 auction.

Two school-section parcels at the October 1833 auction. The town holds one Clybourne and so does the register; Andreas's roster gives the trade, butcher, and explains in the same clause why the household's division is outside_town — he lived north of the limits and could not vote in the village. A family assessed in the county since the 1820s and named on the town's own rolls in 1833 is not a stranger the surname happened to match.

All three tokens agree, which is exactly what carried FRAME DAVID P in T-0700. The register prints COLE PARKER M; the Chicago Democrat's letter list of 9 July 1834 prints 'Parker M. Cole'. The card began as a letter-list identity, and under this file's own rule that would refuse it — but the clause refuses a BARE name read once off a letter list, and this one is not bare: the middle initial is printed by the post office and by the land office alike, and the town's rolls and three later directories hold the man after. The register holds one Cole.

A documented tavern keeper at Wolf Point, printed by name in the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 and keeping the house that was the district polling place on 9 December 1833 — the town has him in residence in the weeks around the 24 October 1833 school-section parcel, and again in June 1835 for the federal entry in T39N R13E. One Ingersoll in the register, one in the layer, and the forename agrees in full.

Two school-section parcels of October 1833. The town holds one Lloyd and the register holds one; beyond the name there are two independent documents around the entry — a contemporary Chicago paper naming him in the town, and Norris's directory of 1844 naming him still there eleven years after the auction. Two documents on the town's side is what this file's rule asks for where there is no initial and no trade to check.

Four rows, the forename in full, one Pruyne in the register and one in the layer. Andreas and the history of medicine in Chicago both hold him as a druggist in the town, and Fergus 1839 prints him at the city election of 1837 — so the town's record spans the 1833 auction and the 1835 federal entry alike.

An initial alone would not carry it. What carries it is the PEARSONS H argument: the SAME register spells this purchaser PRUYNE PETER on four other rows, one of them at the same auction two days earlier, and the town holds no second Pruyne for the initial to belong to. The single school-section parcel of 25 October 1833 is the same hand the register writes out in full elsewhere.

Eleven federal entries and 1,360 acres between 26 June and 16 October 1835, the largest single block in this cohort. The town's tax list of 1833 names a Jeremiah Price, and Fergus 1839, Fergus 1843 and Norris 1844 all hold him after — four documents beyond the register, spanning the year of the purchases on both sides. The register spells the surname one way only and the layer holds one Price.

Three school-section parcels on 22 October 1833. The town's own polls of 1834 and 1835 both print 'Steele, Ashbel', Andreas gives the trade, plasterer, and neither register nor layer holds a second Steele. An unusual forename printed identically by the land office and by the town's clerk is a token, not a coincidence of surname.

The register's own Residence column, which is the strongest thing this source ever offers and what carried DILL FRANK in T-0700: three of these four rows state COOK. A man of this name was of Cook County when he entered 320 acres in October and December 1834, and a contemporary Chicago paper names John Ludby in the town on 19 November 1834, between the two entries. Fergus 1839 and 1843 hold him after. One Ludby in the register, one in the layer.

The card is a letter-list identity, which this file's rule refuses where the name is bare — and this one is not bare. The Democrat's return of 2 July 1834 prints 'Henry c. West' and the register prints WEST HENRY C: the middle initial is on both sides, which is exactly the FRAME DAVID P ruling of T-0700 and exactly what SPENCER WILLIAM G lacked when it was refused, its initial being one the town had never seen. West is a common surname and the initial is what narrows it; without that token this would be refused with the other letter-list four.

One canal entry of 29 September 1830, and on the town's side one line of the 1833 tax list and nothing else — a G3 identity, read once and corroborated by nothing. Two bare names three years apart, and no initial, trade, or second document between them. The residence column reads ILLINOIS, which is a state and does not reach the town. The proposal rests on the residents layer holding exactly one Hartzell, which is a fact about the layer and not about these two records agreeing. A second reading naming him — a deed, a directory, a paper — would overturn it.

One school-section parcel; on the town's side one line of the 1833 tax list and nothing else. Two things make the refusal firmer than the thinness alone. The register itself holds a SECOND man of this surname — VANDERBOGERT JOHN AS, an assignment — so the surname does not single anyone out even on the page. And the town's own spelling of this family is under an open question: T-0842 asks whether Van Den Bogart and Van der Bogart are one man printed two ways or two men, with a card minted for the second. Ruling an identity onto a name whose identity is itself the open ticket is the order this project does not work in.

Five school-section parcels on 24 October 1833, and on the town's side a single line of the 1833 tax list — G3, read once, corroborated by nothing. The surname is unique in both the register and the layer, and that is the whole of the case: rarity makes the coincidence unlikely, and unlikely is not checked. Nothing on the card can be put against the page — no initial, no trade, no second document, and a residence column reading UNKNOWN on all five rows. Refused with Hartzell and Vanderbogert as one class: one bare-name reading on each side.

Twenty-six school-section parcels, and the register's own pages are what refuse this. HALE EBENEZER enters every one of those parcels as well — the twenty-six duplicate entries T-0885 filed, two names on one parcel on one day on one page of volume 818 — and whether that pair is one transaction or two is a question this project has explicitly left open with the evidence beside it. Against that, the town's side holds one newspaper reading of a very common forename and surname, with no initial and no trade. Writing twenty-six purchases onto John Hale's card would decide T-0885 by default, in the direction that flatters the reconstruction. Refused until it is decided.

The town's man is James C Spence and the register prints SPENCE JAMES — no middle initial at all. So the one token that could be checked sits on the town's side only, which is the mirror of the SPENCER WILLIAM G refusal and fails for the same reason: an initial that appears on one record and not the other tests nothing. Behind the name the card is G2a, the 1835 poll list alone, and the poll's own bound falls after the scene date. Four rows over two years against a bare James Spence is not enough.

One school-section parcel of four acres, 24 October 1833. The town knows this person from ONE return of uncalled-for letters, printed 'Joveph Chandler' in the Democrat of 8 April 1834 — six months AFTER the entry — and the corroboration that lifted the card is a 'J. Chandler' at the city election of May 1837, which the card itself says is evidence of continued residence and not of anything in 1833. Neither offers a token to check the register against, and Joseph Chandler is a common name. This is the clause T-0700 wrote for SPENCER and WILSON.

Five school-section parcels for $663, and on the town's side one return of uncalled-for letters — printed 'Paul Kingston “74.1' in the Democrat of 1 April 1834, six months after the auction — plus later research rows that corroborate the person without printing anything the register can be put against. The register also holds KINGSTON J T and KINGSTON JOHN T, so the surname is not singling this buyer out on the page either. A correspondent believing a name reachable at Chicago and a name entering five parcels are two bare names.

The closest call in this cohort, and it goes the same way. The Democrat's letter list of 20 May 1835 prints 'Minard, Ira 2'; the register enters an Ira Minard on 161 acres in T40N R14E five weeks later, on 27 June 1835. The proximity is striking and it is not a check: the card is a letter-list identity with nothing else on it, no initial, no trade, no second document, and the residence column reads UNKNOWN on both rows. Upholding here would be upholding a coincidence of date, which is the register telling us when somebody bought, not who. One further reading naming Ira Minard in the town would carry it.

T-0700 refused GARRETT A ET CO as a firm and expected this spelling to stand alone on the card. It does not stand. The town has never read this man's forename: the corpus prints 'A. Garrett' — and, garbled, 'A. Gatren' and 'GARRETT' — in four numbers of the American and the Democrat, and an initial is LESS than the bare name the refusal clause was written for. The register offers Augustus, which is a full forename the town cannot check against anything it holds; that is the SPENCER WILLIAM G shape exactly. The trade does not rescue it either: an auctioneer is consistent with any land transaction whatever, which is what makes it useless as a discriminator, unlike the register of the land office that carried WHITLOCK JAMES. So A. Garrett's card carries no land purchase at all, and that is the honest state of it. One printing of the forename in full — a directory line, a deed, an advertisement signed out — would overturn this at once.

UPHELD on the middle name, which the town prints in full and the register prints three ways. The card reads F Gantry Blanchard because the town's own directories print him so: Fergus 1843 has 'Blanchard, Francis Gurtrey, capitalist, res 45 Wells', Fergus 1839 'Blanchard, Francis G., real estate dealer, Lake street', Norris 1844 'Blanchard, Francis G.' — one man, forename Francis, middle name Gurtrey, which is the token this card carries as Gantry. The register spells the same man BLANCHARD F G, BLANCHARD F G AS, BLANCHARD FRANCIS G and BLANCHARD GURTREY, and every one of those is a reading of Francis Gurtrey. So the initial that fired the mechanical rule is not what carries the ruling: what carries it is a middle name the town prints out loud and the register repeats, on a surname the layer holds three of. The trade agrees too — a real estate dealer of 1839 is what a man who bought school-section town lots in the sale of October 1833 becomes, and that is a consistency rather than a proof. THE THING THIS RULING DOES NOT DECIDE: the residents layer holds a SECOND card, Gantry Blanchard, and on this reading the two are very likely one man. That is a duplicate-card question, filed as T-0993 beside T-0844's cluster of six; this ruling rules only that the register's F G is the card the crosswalk named.

The card reads F Gantry Blanchard because the town's own directories print him so: Fergus 1843 has 'Blanchard, Francis Gurtrey, capitalist, res 45 Wells', Fergus 1839 'Blanchard, Francis G., real estate dealer, Lake street', Norris 1844 'Blanchard, Francis G.' — one man, forename Francis, middle name Gurtrey, which is the token this card carries as Gantry. This spelling is the same day and the same block as ls0073 — lot 2 of block 26 against lot 7 — and the trailing AS is the register's own token, carried as the clerk wrote it and not read as part of a name.

The card reads F Gantry Blanchard because the town's own directories print him so: Fergus 1843 has 'Blanchard, Francis Gurtrey, capitalist, res 45 Wells', Fergus 1839 'Blanchard, Francis G., real estate dealer, Lake street', Norris 1844 'Blanchard, Francis G.' — one man, forename Francis, middle name Gurtrey, which is the token this card carries as Gantry. Here the register prints the forename in full, Francis, which is the word Fergus 1839 and Norris 1844 print; the abbreviation is on the town's side of this pair, not the register's.

UPHELD on a forename too odd to be a coincidence of initials, printed on both sides. The card reads S. Foot because the Democrat prints '§. FOOT' and Norris 1844 'Foot, S. teamster' — but Fergus 1839 and 1843 print the word itself: 'Foot, Star, teamster' and 'Foot, Starr, teamster, 180 Clark, cor Monroe'. The register's STAN is a fifth reading of Star/Starr, one letter apart in a transcription-mediated deposit, and not a fourth Christian name beginning with S. That is a token beyond the bare initial and it is what carries the ruling. The register's own arrangement agrees: the two Foots it holds, FOOT JOHN and FOOT STAN, take four consecutive lots of block 117 on one day, 22 October 1833 — John lots 5 and 6, Stan lots 3 and 4 — and the residents layer independently holds exactly two Foots, John and this one. THE LATER DIRECTORIES ARE USED HERE FOR THE NAME AND NOTHING ELSE: 'teamster' is a trade of 1839 and is not back-projected onto 1835, and the card's 1835 trade stays the paper's.

REFUSED against C Goodrich. The town's whole record of that person is one line of the 1833 tax list — an initial and a surname, no trade, no street, no second document, no directory entry in 1839, 1843 or 1844 — and the card says so itself: a projected resident, documented once and corroborated by nothing else, the weakest rung of the ratified ladder. The register prints CHAUNCEY, a forename the town has never seen, and there is nothing on the town's side for it to be checked against. The mechanical rule reached this card because the initial C picked it out of the three Goodriches the layer holds, which is a fact about the layer and not about the man. That both records put a Goodrich at Chicago in 1833 does not close the gap: the school-section sale of October 1833 and the tax list of the same year are the two places a Chicago Goodrich would appear whether or not he is the same Goodrich. Four rows are retracted — lot 4 of block 48 and blocks 130, 131 and 132, $489 of ground.

UPHELD, and the register settles it without leaving the deposit. The same register prints HADDOCK EDWARD H twice — ls0172, lot 7 of block 120, 25 October 1833, three days after the E H rows and inside the same school-section sale, and ls0669 in the country in 1835 — so the abbreviation and the full forename are one hand at one sale. The middle initial H stands on both sides: the town prints 'Haddock, Edward H., commission merchant, South Water st' in Fergus 1839 and John Wentworth's old-settler roll in the Tribune of 25 April 1882 carries 'Edward H. Haddock'. The card is the layer's strongest kind — seven sources, Andreas, the 1840 census, the Democrat — and the layer's only other Haddock is an H Haddock the forename refuses. Nothing here regrades the card or asserts a residence: it was already a documented townsman, and what the ruling adds is that these three rows are his.

UPHELD on the middle initial, which a contemporary Chicago paper prints and the register repeats. The Democrat of 31 December 1833, column 2, names him 'J. W. REED.' and gives his trade as cabinet maker — that is the town's own record, not a later directory — and the register prints REED JAMES W. Two tokens agree, not one: the W refuses George, Thomas and William Reed, and the forename refuses S W Reed, who is the only other Reed in the layer carrying a W. The register's other Reeds are ROBERT and THOMAS, and it never spells this purchaser any other way. The three lots are one day, 25 October 1833, inside the school-section sale. The household this person sits on is a reconstructed roof raised by the occupation census and this ruling does not touch it: it rules on the man, not the dwelling.

UPHELD, and like Haddock the register expands its own abbreviation: WRIGHT TRUMAN G appears twice in the same deposit, ls0518 and ls0566, both 27 June 1835 in T40N R14E. The middle initial G is on both sides — the card reads Truman G Wright off the tax list of 1833, the poll of 1834, a letter list and the old-settler death notices — and it is what refuses the five other Wrights the layer holds, of whom three are Johns. The trade agrees in the strongest way this domain allows: Fergus 1839 prints 'Wright, Truman G., speculator, bds Tremont House', and six lots and blocks taken in block 70 and around it over three days of the October 1833 school-section sale — $1,282 of town ground in one week — is a speculator at work and not a householder buying somewhere to live. The word speculator is 1839's and is not written onto the 1835 card; it is used here to check an identity, which is what this file is for.

UPHELD on the initials as the town itself prints them, and on a date only one Beaubien can reach. The town's record of this man does not hold a forename it has to have expanded for it: Andreas's 1833 roster prints 'J. B. Beaubien, merchant' and Fergus 1839 prints 'Beaubien, John B., Michigan ave., bet. Lake and So. Water sts' — J. B. is the form the town used, and the register's BEAUBIEN J B is that form. The layer holds ten Beaubiens and the sale is dated 29 September 1830: this card's arrival is attested at 1812 from Andreas — 'he came to Chicago and bought the cabin and cultivated field south of the old fort in 1812' — and it is the only Beaubien in the layer the record puts at Chicago that early. Four canal rows in section 29 of T39N R14E, two of them the register's own voided duplicates of the other two, carried at 212.61 acres and $1,063.20 net. TWO THINGS THIS DOES NOT DO: it does not touch the Fort Dearborn reservation claim, which this project holds no record of and makes no finding on, and it does not make the 1830 purchase evidence of residence — the Residence column reads ILLINOIS on the voided pair and UNKNOWN on the pair that stood, and neither names a town.

REFUSED against L W Smith, on the same ground as SPENCER WILLIAM G under T-0700. The town's whole record of L W Smith is one line of the poll of 1834 — the card calls itself a projected resident, documented once and corroborated by nothing else — with no trade, no street, no second document and no entry in any of the three directories. The register offers LIMAN, and the very next row, ls0573, offers SIMAN for the same tract on the same day at a price one cent apart: the deposit itself does not know whether the man was a Lyman or a Simon, so the token the mechanical rule matched on is not stable in the source that supplies it. The register's row carries no middle initial at all, so the W — the one token that could discriminate among the eleven Smiths the layer holds — is checked against nothing. The COOK in the Residence column sits on the SIMAN reading, not this one, and Cook County in 1834 reaches far beyond the town. One row retracted, 140.18 acres in T38N R14E section 2.

UPHELD, and this is the cleanest in the cohort: the register's forename is the town's own printed forename. Fergus 1843 has 'Montgomery, Loton W., shoemaker, Jerome Beecher, res Market', and the register prints MONTGOMERY LOTON WM and MONTGOMERY LOTON W — Loton is not a name the deposit could have arrived at from an initial. The 1835 card itself rests on the Democrat, which prints 'L. W. MONTGOMERY' in five issues between 17 December 1833 and 20 May 1835 and gives the trade as boot and shoe maker, so the middle initial W is contemporary and not borrowed from 1843. The layer's only other Montgomery is a W Montgomery the forename refuses, and the register's only other is a JOHN whose Residence reads MCLEAN. Eighty acres of the east half of the south-east quarter of section 22, T38N R14E, on 24 November 1835 — the land rush, well south of the town, and the ruling asserts nothing about where he lived.

UPHELD on the same ground as MONTGOMERY LOTON WM: Fergus 1843's 'Montgomery, Loton W., shoemaker' is the register's forename printed by the town, and the Democrat carries L. W. Montgomery through five issues of 1833–1835 with the trade. This is the earlier of his two entries — the north-west quarter of section 23, T38N R14E, 160 acres at $200 on 27 June 1835 — and it sits five months before and one section east of the other, which is one man buying twice in the rush rather than two readings of one sale.

REFUSED against T. M. Morrison, and refused on the rule's own named case. The town holds nothing but 'Morrison, T. M.' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office, the Democrat of 20 May 1835, column 13 — no trade, no street, no household, no directory entry — and an uncalled-for letter says only that a correspondent thought the name reachable at Chicago. The M does appear on both sides, and that is the argument for upholding it; it does not carry, because the M is not a second reading of the man, it is one more character of the same single line, printed by the same list that supplies the T. The register adds THOS, which the town has never seen, and the layer holds five Morrisons — one of them Orsemus Morrison, a documented townsman who bought three town lots at the school-section sale, which is what a Morrison in this register looks like when the town really knows him. The ground here is a fractional quarter in T38N R15E section 32, the far south-east corner of the ring, 78.94 acres, and one row is retracted.

UPHELD, and the register proves it against itself. ls0919 — HUNTER E E, the north-east quarter of section 13, T40N R13E, 80 acres, $100, 15 November 1834 — and ls0920 — HUNTER EDWARD E, the same quarter of the same section on the same day at the same price — are one entry read twice, and the fuller reading states COOK in the Residence column where the abbreviated one leaves it UNKNOWN. So the expansion of E E to EDWARD E is the deposit's, not this ruling's, and it comes with the one column that speaks to residence. The middle initial E is on the town's side as well: the card is attested at G1b off the Democrat, the poll of 1834 and the old-settler death notices, and Fergus 1839 prints him as deputy-sheriff and ex-justice of the peace on Wells street. The layer's four other Hunters are refused on the forename. COOK is a county and not a town, and this ruling reads it as the register's word for the county, exactly as the domain's grading rule does.

NAMED, NOT UPHELD — the mechanical rule never proposed this one and could not. `namesake.choose` weighs the FIRST forename token, and the register prints this man's MIDDLE name in the forename's place, so GURTREY was put to all the Blanchards the town holds and named none of them. What names him is the town's own directory: Fergus 1843 prints 'Blanchard, Francis Gurtrey, capitalist, res 45 Wells [died, Brooklyn, N.Y., 1872.]' — forename Francis, middle name Gurtrey — and Fergus 1839 and Norris 1844 print the same man 'Francis G.' GURTREY is that middle name, and the card carries it as Gantry because the poll of 1834 prints him 'Blanchard, F. Gantry'. THE REGISTER PROVES ITS OWN HABIT HERE, AT ONE SALE. The six GURTREY rows (purchase nos 0367525-0367530, volume 817 page 027) and the three F G rows (0376893-0376895, volume 818 page 010) are the SAME school section — section 16, T39N R14E, type SC — entered on 22 and 24 October 1833, the days the school section was sold off by lot and by block. One buyer, one auction, two volumes of the register, two renderings of one name; the domain's README already records this habit under T-0990, where HUNTER E E and HUNTER EDWARD E are the same 80 acres of section 13 on the same day at the same price. WHAT IS NOT NAMED BY IT. The town's other documented Blanchard is W. G. Blanchard, the house-and-land agent of the Democrat of 9 July 1834, and his forename initial is W: he is refused on the same ground the crosswalk refuses him against every other Blanchard reading. Joseph Blanchard the blacksmith is a man of the directories and not an 1835 resident. Nothing reached prints a second Gurtrey Blanchard anywhere. AND IT IS STILL A PURCHASE. The Residence column reads UNKNOWN on all six rows, so this names a buyer and never an occupant, and it places nobody on that ground. The six rows are lot 1 of block 2, block 21, lot 8 of block 141, block 3, lot 7 of block 82 and lot 1 of block 141 of the school section, $547.00 in all (ls0076-ls0081). Two of them state a price per acre of 3.69 against 0000.00 acres, which is the acreage of the F G row ls0074 standing in the wrong column of the deposit; it is carried as the register has it and read as no acreage at all.

UPHELD, on cohort A's discriminator: the town's card holds only initials — J. K. Botsford — and the directories print the forename whole. Fergus 1839 has 'Botsford, Jabez K., Botsford & Beers', Fergus 1843 'Botsford, Jabez Kent (B. & Beers), 109 Lake', Norris 1844 'Botsford, J. K. of B. & Beers'. The register writes JABEZ K, which is the 1839 line exactly, so the forename and the middle initial are both checked against a printing the town holds rather than against the initial the mechanical rule matched on. The card is attested at a TRADE besides — sheet iron worker, stove manufacturer, tinsmith, at the Democrat of 10 September 1834 — and a tinsmith with a shop taking two school-section blocks at the sale of 24 October 1833 is a townsman buying town ground. Nothing here says he lived on either block: what is carried is that he entered them.

UPHELD, and by the same route. The town's card is J. K. Boyer; Fergus 1839 prints 'Boyer, John K., coroner, South Water street near Clark', which supplies the forename AND repeats the middle initial, and the register writes JOHN K. The card is on the poll lists and in the Democrat as well, so the man is held at Chicago across the nine school-section lots of 22 and 25 October 1833 and the 80 acres of 13 June 1835. The 1839 trade is not read back onto 1835 — the card's own occupation stays none_recorded with the coronership in later_occupation, and this ruling does not touch it.

UPHELD. The middle initial is on both sides and the town's record is one of the densest it holds: Andreas's 1833 roster has 'George W. Dole, merchant', the Democrat of 26 November 1833 carries the forwarding and commission firm's own advertisement, and the directories print him George W. in 1839, George Washington in 1843 and Geo. W. in 1844. The register writes DOLE GEORGE W. He is the only George W. Dole in either record, he is documented in the town in the same season as the school-section sale of October 1833, and a forwarding merchant taking a block and two lots at that sale is the purchase the record would predict. The register's other Dole spelling, the bare DOLE, is a different reading and is not touched by this ruling.

UPHELD, and on the bracket rather than on an initial — the register gives no middle initial here, and this ruling does not pretend otherwise. What carries it is that the forename agrees IN FULL on a surname each record holds exactly once, and that the town holds Alexander N. Fullerton continuously across both entry dates in eight sources: Andreas counts him one of the six lawyers who had put out a sign by the close of 1833, which is the month of the school-section lots of 24 and 25 October 1833, and the American of 1835, the Democrat and the poll lists hold him through the summer of the ring entries of 26 June 1835. The directories then print him whole — Alex. N., Alexander Nathaniel, A. N. — on the same Dearborn street address. Both entry dates are bracketed by documents that put this man in this town; that is the rule's second limb and not a bare-name coincidence. No residence on any of the six parcels is asserted.

UPHELD. The register writes GOODHUE JOSIAH C and Fergus 1839 prints 'Goodhue, Dr. Josiah C., Dearborn street north of Lake street' — forename, middle initial and honorific, the same three tokens in the same order. The card is attested at a trade off the Democrat of 4 February 1834, physician, and is held again on the poll lists and in the old-settler death notices. One Goodhue in the register and one in the layer. The single lot — lot 4 of block 119, taken at the school-section sale of 25 October 1833 for $253 — is carried as an entry and not as a dwelling; the card's placement is unchanged.

UPHELD. The card carries the initial only, W. Kimball, and Fergus 1839 prints 'Kimball, Walter, probate judge, cor. Clark and South Water st' — the forename whole, at the corner the card already holds him at, because his own signed advertisement in the Democrat of 26 November 1833 opens a New Store for dry goods at the corner of South Water and Clark. The register writes WALTER. A merchant with a store at that corner taking lot 2 of block 49 at the school-section sale of 25 October 1833 is consistent with everything the town holds of him, and the Calumet Club and Tribune old-settler notices hold him after. The layer's other Kimball reading, Wm. Kimbal, disagrees on the forename and is not this man.

UPHELD, and the middle initial is on the TOWN's side, not only the register's: the card's press reading is 'E. S. Kimberley' in the Democrat of 1 July 1835, and the 1840 census reads 'Ed. Kimberley' — two independent documents bracketing the scene date, the earlier of them printing the S the register repeats when it writes KIMBERLEY EDMUND S. That is the NEWBERRY WALTER L check of T-0700 and not a bare name. WHAT THE RULING ALSO FOUND, and it is why the crosswalk reported no rival: the layer ALSO holds `kimberly_edmund_s`, Dr Edmund Stoughton Kimberly, attested off Andreas, the poll lists and a medical history, printed 'Kimberly, Dr. Edmund S.' in Fergus 1839 and 'Kimberly, Edmund Stoughten, physician' in Fergus 1843 — the same forename and the same middle initial, spelled Kimberly rather than Kimberley. tools/namesake.py folds surnames exactly, so it never gathered him and `rivals[]` came back empty on a proposal that has a namesake in every sense but the spelling. The two cards are very probably one man, which makes this a card question and not an identity question — the purchaser is that man on either reading — so the entry is upheld here and the duplicate is filed as its own ticket, exactly as cohort A upheld the three Blanchard spellings and filed T-0993.

UPHELD on the middle initial, which is the rule's first limb and is unusually safe here. The town's card is A V Knickerbacker off the poll lists, Norris 1844 prints 'Knickerbacker, A. V. grocery and provisions, South Water st', and the register writes ABRM V — the same middle initial V, with the forename expanded to a reading of Abraham the register supplies and the town does not. The surname is uncommon enough that the register holds it once and the layer holds it once, and the V agrees where a bare A would have decided nothing. Lot 1 of block 72 and block 101, entered 22 and 23 October 1833 at the school-section sale, are carried as entries. The 1844 grocery is not read back onto 1835 and the card's occupation is untouched.

UPHELD, on three initials rather than one. The register writes PECK P F W; the town holds Philip F. W. Peck off Andreas's 1833 roster — 'P. F. W. Peck, merchant' — and the directories print him Philip F. W. in 1839, Philip Ferdinand Wheeler in 1843 and P. F. W. in 1844. A three-initial string agreeing token for token is not a coincidence the bare-name rule has to worry about. He is a merchant with a two-storey store at South Water and LaSalle in the season of the school-section sale, and blocks 116 and 6 taken on 23 and 24 October 1833 are the purchase that record predicts. The register's other Peck, PECK EBENEZER, is a different man and is not touched. Nothing is asserted about where he lived.

UPHELD, on the forename and the trade together. The card is J. Shrigley, attested at a trade off the Democrat of 8 October 1834 — tavern keeper — and Fergus 1839 prints 'Shrigley, John, tavern keeper', which supplies the forename the register writes and repeats the trade the card already held. Fergus 1843 holds him still. One Shrigley in the register, one in the layer, and the town's own record independently attests both tokens the proposal turned on. The 80 acres in T40N R14E entered on 27 June 1835 are carried as an entry; a tavern keeper's premises are in the town and this ruling does not move them.

UPHELD. The card holds a trade attested off the Democrat of 13 August 1834, provision dealer, and the directories print both the forename and the continuation of that trade: Fergus 1843 'Marsh, Sylvester, 98 Lake, packing-house, 304-6 North Water', Norris 1844 the same. The register writes SYLVESTER, which is the directories' spelling rather than the card's Silvester, so the printing the ruling checks against is the one that agrees with the register letter for letter. A provision dealer who becomes a packer is the trade a man buying 160 acres in T38N R14E in June 1835 and two more eighties in February 1836 is buying ground for, and the surname is held once in each record. The card's occupation and its placement are untouched: what is carried is that he entered the parcels.

UPHELD, and this is the line the cohort's refusals are drawn against. The town holds L. T. Jamison TWICE and independently — the Democrat of 4 June 1834 and the poll of 1835, both graded G1a, both printing the same two initials — so the record brackets the scene date instead of resting on one reading. The register writes LOUIS T: it repeats the middle initial T, which is the rule's first limb, and expands the L to a forename the town has not seen. Where the same expansion appears in this cohort on a card that holds ONE name-only line, it has been refused; here the initial pair is attested on two documents of different kinds, one of them a poll list, which is the NEWBERRY WALTER L shape of T-0700. The two entries of December 1835 and January 1836 are carried as entries and assert no residence on either tract.

REFUSED against A. Chipman, on the SPENCER WILLIAM G ground of T-0700. The card is marked `letter_list_only`: the town's whole record of this person is one line of the Democrat's return of uncalled-for letters at 1 July 1835 — no trade, no street, no second document, no directory entry in 1839, 1843 or 1844 — and the household around them was written, in its own words, to claim nothing. The register supplies ANSEL, a forename the town has never seen, and the mechanical rule fired because the layer holds exactly one Chipman, which is a fact about how thin the layer is. THE RESIDENCE COLUMN WAS WEIGHED AND DOES NOT CARRY IT: ls0001 and its twin are one entry read twice, and the fuller reading states COOK. That is what upheld DILL FRANK in T-0700 — but there the town's side was a poll list, a document that says a man lived in the place, and here it is a letter somebody had not called for. A COOK entry and an uncalled-for letter are two name-only readings that agree about a county, and the rule refuses those however unlikely the coincidence looks. The 80 acres in section 4, T39N R14E are retracted.

REFUSED against Edmund Roberts. The forename agrees in full, and nothing else does. The town's record is the 1833 tax list — 'Roberts, Edmund', graded G3 — and a Second Presbyterian retrospect of 1892: two name-only readings, no trade, no street, no middle initial, no directory line in any of the three volumes. The register's row carries no middle initial either, so there is no token for the town's side to be checked against. Two things make it worse rather than better. The entry is dated 5 OCTOBER 1830, three years before the earliest reading the town holds of this man, and nothing brackets that gap. And the surname is not rare in the source that supplies it: the same register sells to ROBERTS CHARLES and ROBERTS MARY, so the layer holding exactly one Roberts is a fact about the layer and not about Cook County. The 40 acres in section 9, T39N R14E are retracted.

REFUSED against J Stanley, on the GOODRICH CHAUNCEY ground of cohort A. The town's whole record is one line of the 1833 tax list — 'Stanley, J.', graded G3, an initial and a surname — with no trade, no street, no second document and no entry in Fergus 1839, Fergus 1843 or Norris 1844. The register prints JOSEPH, a forename the town has never seen, and there is nothing on the town's side for it to be checked against. The mechanical rule reached this card because the initial J is the only Stanley the layer holds. That both records put a Stanley at Chicago in 1833 does not close the gap: the school-section sale of October 1833 and the tax list of the same year are the two places a Chicago Stanley would appear whether or not he is the same Stanley. Lot 4 of block 118, $131.50, is retracted.

REFUSED against Herman A. Rowley, and the agreeing middle initial is the reason this one needed saying. The card is `letter_list_only`: one line of the Democrat's uncalled-for letters at 20 May 1835, printing 'Rowley, Herman A.' — an initial pair and nothing else, no trade, no street, no second document, no directory line. The register writes HEMAN A, so the A does agree, and the forename differs by a letter that either hand could have made. A MIDDLE INITIAL DISCRIMINATES; IT DOES NOT CORROBORATE. In T-0700 the L of NEWBERRY WALTER L decided among candidates the town already held in the American of 1835 and both Fergus directories; here it is the whole of the town's record, and two name-only readings do not make an identity because one of them is fuller than the other. The 160 acres in section 6, T40N R14E, entered 27 June 1835, are retracted.

REFUSED against N F Hurd, on the same reading of the middle initial as ROWLEY HEMAN A above. The town's record is a single press line — 'N. F. Hurd' in the Democrat of 25 June 1834, graded G1b — with no trade, no street, no second document and no directory entry. The register writes NIRAM F: the F agrees and the forename is one the town has never seen, so the agreeing token is the same token the mechanical rule matched on and the expansion is checked against nothing. The register settles the other half of it directly — it also sells to HURD DENNIS S, so Cook County held at least two Hurds while the layer held one, and the uniqueness the rule leaned on is a property of the layer. The two parcels in section 30, T38N R15E, entered 27 June 1835, are retracted.

REFUSED against Tho's Allison. The card is `letter_list_only`: a letter was still waiting for this name at the Democrat of 1 July 1835 and that is the entire record — no trade, no street, no second document, no directory line. The forename agrees, and agreement on a forename is what the mechanical rule already had. The Residence column states COOK on this row, which is the strongest thing the register offers and which upheld DILL FRANK and LUDBY JOHN; in both of those the town's side was a document of residence or a newspaper naming the man in the town between his entries, and here it is a letter nobody called for. A tract entry by a Cook County Thomas Allison in April 1835 and an uncalled-for letter addressed to a Chicago Thomas Allison in July are two name-only readings that agree about a county. The 160 acres in section 30, T40N R14E are retracted.

REFUSED against J. L. Sackett. The card is `letter_list_only` — one line of the Democrat's uncalled-for letters at 2 July 1834, an initial pair and a surname, and the card's own note says the corpus stops before the scene date. The register writes SACKETT JOSHUA, which agrees with the J and carries NO middle initial at all, so the L — the one token that could have discriminated — is checked against nothing, and the forename Joshua is one the town has never seen. This is SPENCER WILLIAM G with the disagreement on the other side of the name. The 80 acres in section 32, T40N R14E, entered 30 May 1835, are retracted.

REFUSED against Catherine Ostrander, and with some regret, because a woman entering 79.46 acres in her own name in May 1835 is worth more than the record can carry. The card is `letter_list_only`: one line of the Democrat's uncalled-for letters at 22 October 1834, no trade, no street, no second document, and the card's own present_on_scene_date reads `uncertain` because nothing follows her to 1 July 1835. The forename agrees; the register's F in the social-status column confirms the register's own reading of its own row and says nothing about the town's. Two name-only readings. The parcel in section 4, T38N R14E is retracted, and the register's entry stands on its own as a woman's purchase in Cook County — it is the identification with the town's Catherine Ostrander that is refused, not the purchase.

REFUSED against B Blaisdell. The town's whole record is one line of the poll of 1835 — 'Blaisdell, B.', graded G2a — with no trade, no street, no second document and no directory entry, and the card's arrival bound falls AFTER the scene date, so even the town's one reading does not place him there on 1 July 1835. The register prints BENJAMIN, a forename the town has never seen, checked against an initial. That is the GOODRICH CHAUNCEY shape exactly. The 160 acres in section 24, T38N R14E, entered 27 June 1835, are retracted.

REFUSED against A. Shepherd. The card is `letter_list_only` — the Democrat's uncalled-for letters at 2 July 1834, one line, no trade, no street, no second document, nothing following him to the scene date. The register prints ALBERT against the town's bare A. The layer holding one Shepherd is what fired the rule and is a fact about the layer. The 80 acres in section 32, T38N R14E, entered 27 June 1835, are retracted.

REFUSED against D Wilcox. The town's record is one press line — 'Capt. D. Wilcox' in the Democrat of 4 February 1834, graded G1b — and the honorific is a rank, not a check: the register's social-status column is blank on all three of these rows, so there is nothing on its side for a captaincy to agree with. What the register does print is DE LA FAYETTE, as distinctive a forename as this cohort contains and one the town has never seen, reduced by the mechanical rule to the initial D. A striking name checked against a single letter is the weakest reading the rule admits, not the strongest. The three parcels in sections 32, 33 and 34 of T38N R14E, entered between December 1835 and March 1836, are retracted.

REFUSED against Thomas Church, and not because the man is a stranger — the directories hold him firmly enough, a grocer at 109-111 Lake through 1839, 1843 and 1844. Two things refuse it. The register writes THOS JR, and the JR is the page saying there was ANOTHER Thomas Church of the same county, presumably the father; the town holds one Thomas Church and nothing on its side distinguishes the two, so the one token that discriminates here is checked against nothing. And the town's 1835 record of him is thinner than the directories make it look: the card is written, in its own words, almost entirely to keep a building from being anonymous, its present_on_scene_date says nothing places him in the town on any particular date, and the source that names him names him as the BUILDER of the first store on Lake Street rather than as its occupant. That the identification is probably right is not what is refused. The 160 acres in section 34, T39N R13E, entered 5 August 1835, are retracted.

REFUSED against William Allen. The forename agrees in full and decides nothing: the layer holds three Allens, the register holds this spelling once, and both records are a bare name. What the town holds of him in 1835 is one uncalled-for letter — the Democrat of 1 July 1835, column 4 — and the card says so in the field, `letter_list_only`. The later rows do not rescue it, because they are gathered by the same undiscriminating fold and they disagree with each other: Fergus 1839 prints a William Allen keeping a SALOON on North Canal street south of Kinzie, Fergus 1843 a Wm. Allen SHIPCARPENTER on Wolcott between North Water and Kinzie, Norris 1844 the shipwright of the same Wolcott street address. Two trades and two neighbourhoods is the fold gathering more than one man, not one man corroborated; and the 1840 census tick is a name in a column. Nothing on the town's side carries a middle initial, a trade the register's row is what you would predict from, or a date that brackets it. The 80 acres of W2NW sec 14 T38N R14E entered 27 June 1835 for $100.00 are retracted.

UPHELD against Davi Andrews — on the second corpus, not on the letter list. The letter list alone would refuse this: the Democrat of 1 July 1835, column 4, prints 'Andrews, Davi' once, and the card carries `letter_list_only`. What carries it is that the town's record of him is not that reading alone. The 2026 resident-research pass (T-0480) read a retrospective Cook County biography that identifies David Andrews IN COOK COUNTY FROM 1834 and supports exact-name continuity, and it recorded the finding as `corroborated_enrichment` with `asserted_identity` true; that is a document independent of the register, it names the same county the register's rows lie in, and it BRACKETS the entry date from before. Fergus 1839 then prints 'Andrews, David, tailor, north side', a third reading of the same forename in full. Two rows of 26 June 1835 follow — W2NE sec 24 T39N R13E for $320.00 and E2NW sec 36 T39N R13E for $180.00, both above the minimum, 160 acres in all. What is upheld is the IDENTITY of the purchaser and nothing else: the research row says plainly that its evidence does not establish a roof on 1 July 1835, and this ruling asserts no residence.

REFUSED against William Andrews. The town's whole record of him is one line in a Chicago paper — 'Wm. Andrews', the Democrat of 25 June 1834, column 10 — and a name in a newspaper is a name. Fergus 1839's 'Andrews, William, tailor, north side' adds a trade of 1839 and no address, and it sits one line from 'Andrews, David, tailor, north side': the same trade at the same side of town for two forenames is a fold this ruling cannot lean on. The register's own hand is unsteady on this surname in the same week — it enters ANDREWS WILLAIM at E2SEFR sec 08 T40N R14E on 27 June 1835 and ANDREWS WILLIAM at E2SE sec 17 T40N R14E on the same day, two distinct tracts under two spellings of one name — so the register is not offering a second, fuller reading to check the first against. Residence column UNKNOWN. Two name-only readings do not make an identity. The 80 acres of E2SE sec 17 T40N R14E entered 27 June 1835 for $176.00 are retracted.

UPHELD against William B Archer, on a middle initial that TWO independent town-side documents print. The register writes ARCHER WILLIAM B. The Chicago American of 4 July 1835, column 10, prints 'William B. Archer' in the town; Fergus's old-settler death notices print 'Archer, Col. William B.' The initial B is therefore not a token this project has read once and is now checking against itself — which is what refused ROWLEY HEMAN A and HURD NIRAM F in cohort B — but a token two records of different kinds agree on, and the layer's only rival of the surname is Joseph Archer, whom the forename refuses outright. The newspaper reading falls eight days after the entry of 26 June 1835, so a document brackets the purchase. What is NOT upheld is any claim about the scene: the card's own bound falls after 1 July 1835 and its `present_on_scene_date` reads uncertain, and this ruling leaves both where they are. The entry stands: E2NE sec 22 T39N R13E, 80.00 acres, $160.00, ls0820.

REFUSED against Thomas Ballard. This is the SPENCER WILLIAM G shape in its plainest form. The town holds him exactly once — the 1835 poll list, 'Ballard, Thomas', record poll_1835_003 — with no trade, no street, no household and no arrival; the card grades him G2a on that single list and writes every other field unattested. The register holds him exactly once, 26 June 1835, W2NW sec 36 T39N R13E, 80 acres for $100.00, Residence column UNKNOWN. There is nothing on either side but a name, and the layer holds a second Ballard. A poll list says a man of this name voted at Chicago and a tract entry says a man of this name entered ground; the two agree only in the name. The 80 acres and $100.00 are retracted.

UPHELD against Mark Beaubien, and this one is not close. Ten Beaubiens stand in the layer and the forename Mark chooses one of them: the tavern-keeper of the Sauganash, at whose house the incorporation election of 10 August 1833 was held by the clerk's own printed notice and at whose house the board resolved to meet, one of the twenty-eight electors, named by Andreas, by the Calumet Club's 1879 roll and by Wentworth's 1882 list of old settlers dead since 1881, printed a hotel-keeper on Lake street in Fergus 1839 and the United States light-house keeper in Fergus 1843. The register's two rows are lots 7 and 8 of BLOCK 81 in section 16, bought on 25 October 1833 for $70.00 and $101.00 — town lots at the canal commissioners' school-section sale, in the same town and the same season as every document above, by a man the town's own record shows keeping a house of business in it. The register separately carries BEAUBIEN J B, upheld in cohort A, so the two brothers are distinguished on the register's side as well as the town's. A trade, a premises, a documented presence in the year of the sale: far more than a name.

REFUSED against William Bennett, and the Residence column is what has to be argued with. Two of the four rows read COOK, and cohort B found COOK worth something — but only WITH a town-side partner: it carried DILL FRANK and LUDBY JOHN because a poll list AND a newspaper stood behind them. Here the town holds this man ONCE, on the 1834 poll list, and the card grades him G3 — 'projected resident', the weakest rung the ladder defines, documented once and corroborated by nothing else. Fergus 1839's 'Bennett, William, soap boiler' carries no address and is a trade of 1839; the register's rows are of 1834 and buy nothing a soap boiler is more likely to buy than anyone else. The rows themselves are thinner than four: E2NWVOID sec 20 is a void entry, and the two SE sec 32 T40N R14E rows of 27 December 1834 are one entry read from two volumes. A county of many thousands and one poll line are still one document each. The four rows the card carried — 320 acres and $400.00 as the register counts them, though two of the four are one entry read from two volumes and a third is void — are retracted.

REFUSED against Levi Blake. He has two readings and they are the same reading twice: two returns of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office, the Democrat of 20 May 1835 (printed 'Bleke, Levi') and of 19 August 1835. The card carries `letter_list_only`. An uncalled-for letter says a correspondent believed the name reachable at Chicago; two of them say two correspondents believed it, which is not a second KIND of document and adds nothing the register's row can be checked against — no trade, no street, no initial, no bracketing date, and no directory line in 1839, 1843 or 1844. The register's single row of 27 June 1835, E2NE sec 26 T38N R14E, 80 acres for $108.00, reads UNKNOWN in the Residence column. Retracted.

UPHELD against Erastus Selden Bowen, on two contemporaneous civic lists and the date of the sale. The town assessed an Erastus Bowen on the 1833 TAX LIST and polled him in 1834 — two independent readings of the town's own records, the first of them in the very year of this purchase. The register's row is BL65 in section 16, bought 23 October 1833 for $602.00: a whole block at the canal commissioners' school-section sale, the sale at which the town's own householders bought their ground, and $602 is a sum that says the buyer was there to bid. A man on the Chicago tax list of 1833 buying a block of section 16 in October 1833 is the two records meeting in one place at one time, which is what the rule asks for and what a bare name cannot give. Fergus 1839 then prints him CITY COLLECTOR at South Water and Michigan, Fergus 1843 and Norris 1844 keep him at 40 Michigan avenue, and the Calumet Club's 1879 roll of settlers before 1840 holds him. The forename is distinctive and the layer's only other Bowen is refused on it.

UPHELD against William H Brown, on a middle initial the town prints independently twice. Six Browns stand in the layer and the register sells to four spellings of the surname, so the initial is doing the whole work — and it is corroborated rather than assumed: the Democrat prints 'W. H. Brown' on 28 May 1834 and 'Wm. H. Brown' on 4 June 1834, two separate readings in a contemporary Chicago paper, and Fergus 1839 has 'Brown, William H., cashier, Branch State Bank Illinois, LaSalle st cor. So. Water' where Norris 1844 has 'Brown, William H. attorney, office Bank Building'. That is the JAMISON LOUIS T pattern of cohort B — the town prints the initial pair twice independently — and not the ROWLEY pattern, where the pair IS the record. The Residence column reads ILLINOIS on ls0399. Two things this ruling does NOT say: the entries are of January and June 1831, four years before the scene and two before the town was incorporated, so they place nobody at Chicago and no bound moves; and ls0399 is marked void. E2NE sec 17 T39N R14E, 80 acres, $100.00, stands as this man's.

REFUSED against William H Brown — and refused BY THE REGISTER'S OWN HAND. The same register, for the same surname, writes BROWN WILLIAM H when it has the middle initial; here it writes BROWN WM and stops. A clerk who records the initial elsewhere and omits it here is telling you the initial was not on the paper, so folding WM into WILLIAM H would be reading in the one token that discriminates. There is more than one William Brown to lose him among: the register also holds BROWN JEREMIAH and BROWN RUFUS, the layer holds six Browns, and the directories print at least three distinct men — Fergus 1843's 'Brown, William, grocer, res N. Water', its 'Brown, Wm., bds Sauganash [died, Nevada City, Cal, Dec. 3, 1850.]' and its 'Brown, William Hubbard, [cashier]', with Norris 1844 keeping the grocer, the Sauganash boarder and the attorney apart on three lines. Residence column UNKNOWN on both rows. The 480 acres of E2 sec 31 and SW sec 32 T38N R14E, entered 7 March 1836 for $600.00 in all, are retracted from William H Brown's card.

REFUSED against Paul Burdick. One uncalled-for letter — the Democrat of 1 July 1835, column 4 — is the entire town-side record; the card carries `letter_list_only` and grades him G3, projected resident, documented once and corroborated by nothing. No directory prints him in 1839, 1843 or 1844, no civic list holds him, no trade and no street are recorded. The register's two rows of 9 June 1835 read UNKNOWN in the Residence column and carry nothing but the name, and the surname is not even unique on the register's side: it also sells to BURDICK WILLIAM W, entered a second time as BURDICK WM W. A name in a post-office list against a name in a tract book is exactly the pair the rule refuses. The 160 acres of SW sec 28 T40N R14E and E2NE sec 12 T39N R13E, $200.00 in all, are retracted.

UPHELD against Philo Carpenter, on a trade, a premises and the town's own election records. The forename is distinctive among the layer's three Carpenters, and the man it names is documented contemporaneously and retrospectively: one of the twenty-eight electors of 10 August 1833 with a vote for trustee, one of the nine village citizens among the twenty-six founding members of the First Presbyterian Church of 26 June 1833 and one of its three first elders, named by Andreas in the imperfect list of the denizens of the town, and printed by the Calumet Club among the guests at its 1882 reception for settlers before 1840. Fergus 1839 prints him 'druggist and apothecary, South Water st' and the card already carries his shop. The register's two lots of 22 and 23 October 1833 — BL27 for $157.00 and BL128 for $150.00 in section 16 — are bought at the school-section sale in the same months as the church and the election, by a man the town's records place in it; the third row, SE sec 8 T39N R14E of 23 March 1836, follows the same buyer outward. Fergus 1843 and Norris 1844 then address him at CARPENTER'S ADDITION on West Randolph, which is what the man who bought blocks became. Far more than a name on each side.

UPHELD against Chas. H. Chapman, on the middle initial, the year and the trade together. The town prints the initial pair four times in documents of three kinds: the 1833 TAX LIST as 'Chapman, Charles H.', the Democrat of 26 November 1833 as 'Chapman, C. H.' and of 13 August 1834 as 'Charles H. Chapman', and the Chicago American of 1835. The tax list is the decisive one — it assesses him at Chicago in 1833, the year the register's three lots were bought, on 22 and 25 October 1833 at the school-section sale. And Fergus 1839 prints him 'real estate dealer, Randolph street', which is precisely the trade three scattered town lots — lot 3 of block 141, lot 8 of block 93, lot 4 of block 96, $249.00 in all — are what you would predict from; Fergus 1843 and Norris 1844 keep him on Wells between Randolph and Washington. The layer's only other Chapman is refused on the forename. That the card also carries `letter_list_only` from a 1834 return does not weaken this: the tax list and the newspapers are not letter lists.

REFUSED against John K Clark, and the register itself is the reason. The town's whole record of him is ONE line — 'John K. Clark' in the Chicago American of 11 July 1835, column 7 — dated after both the scene and the November 1834 entries; there is no trade, no street, and no directory line, because Fergus 1839 has 'Clark, John, (Hobbie & Clark)', Fergus 1843 has J. COE CLARK and 'Clark, John D.', and Norris 1844 has J. Coe Clark. So the initial K is the town's entire record beyond the name, which is the ROWLEY HEMAN A refusal exactly. Worse, the register does not agree with itself on it: ls0897 (volume 236, page 042, purchase 0193774) and ls0898 (volume 687, page 193, purchase 0020148) are ONE ENTRY — the same SW sec 11 T40N R13E, the same 80 acres and $100.00 on the same 4 November 1834 — read from two volumes, and the one volume calls the purchaser CLARK JOHN K where the other calls him CLARK JOHN R. A token the source contradicts on its own page cannot decide an identity, whatever the Residence column's COOK adds. (ls0026 and ls0027 are likewise one entry, E2SE sec 06 T39N R14E, read twice.) The three rows the card carried — 240 acres and $300.00 as counted, two real entries of 80 acres behind them — are retracted.

UPHELD against Josiah P Cook, and it is cohort A's lesson used in reverse. The town's 1833 TAX LIST prints him 'Cook, J. P.' — initials only, in the year of the purchase — and Fergus 1843 and Norris 1844 both print the forename WHOLE, 'Josiah P. Cook, baker, res Michigan avenue'. The directories are what turn the tax list's J. P. into this man, so the town holds him three times and twice with the middle initial the register also writes. The initial is load-bearing here because the surname is crowded on both sides: the register sells to COOK CHARLES W, COOK ISAAC and COOK THOMAS besides, and the layer holds five Cooks. The row is lot 7 of block 120, section 16, 25 October 1833 for $45.00 — one of the cheapest town lots in the school-section sale, which is a baker's purchase rather than a speculator's, and bought in the same year the town assessed him. Upheld.

UPHELD against Thomas Cook, on the town holding him four times and on the year. The 1833 TAX LIST assesses a Thomas Cook at Chicago; the register's first row is lot 2 of block 47 in section 16, bought 24 October 1833 for $29.00, the cheapest kind of lot at the school-section sale. Same man, same town, same year, and a sum that fits the trade the directories give him without a break: Fergus 1839 'Cook, Thomas, teamster, Desplaines st near Monroe', Fergus 1843 'teamster, Desplaines, south of Randolph', Norris 1844 'teamster, Desplaines st', with the 1840 census holding him between them. One trade and one street across three directories and eleven years is a continuous man, not a fold gathering strangers — which is the difference between this and the Allen and Andrews refusals in this cohort. The layer's other four Cooks are refused on the forename and the register's other Cooks all carry different ones. The second row, W2SE sec 25 T38N R14E of 27 June 1835, is the same purchaser reaching outside the town and is upheld with it.

retired.reasoning: GARRETT A ET CO is refused against A. Garrett — not because the firm is a stranger, but because the purchaser is a FIRM and this crosswalk proposes correspondences between a purchaser and a PERSON. 'ET CO' is the register saying the buyer was a partnership; the eighty acres in T38N R14E entered on 1 December 1835 were entered by the house, and a card that says this person entered them says something the page does not. The town's A. Garrett is well attested — an auctioneer in four numbers of the American and the Democrat — and the identification of the firm with him is probably right and is not what is refused. Reading firms as entities in their own right, so a partnership's purchase can be recorded against the partnership and its partners named, is T-0851.
retired.retired_because: The last sentence of this ruling's own reasoning named T-0851 as the ticket that would read firms as entities in their own right, and T-0851 did it: tools/namesake.py's firm_style() reads the register's own 'ET CO' and 'AND CO' as the page saying the purchaser was a partnership, and build_resident_crosswalk() refuses every one of them against every person BY RULE, before the surname gathers anybody. So this judgement is now a derivation and a hand ruling on it would be a ruling on nothing — which is what --check called it. The reasoning is kept here rather than deleted: it is the argument the rule was written from, and the second firm the rule caught (PRUYNE P AND CO, whose entry had been written onto Peter Pruyne's card as his own) is what a hand ruling on one spelling could never reach.
